items.claim: The Equal Employment Opportunity Commission may apply the collateral source rule when awarding past pecuniary damages against a federal agency under 42 U.S.C. § 2000e-16(b), thereby declining to deduct insurance benefits received by a claimant through the Federal Employees Health Benefits program.

items.case_name: The Equal Employment Opportunity Commission's Use of the Collateral Source Rule in Federal Sector Discrimination Cases
items.case_holding_text: When the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission awards past pecuniary damages against a federal agency pursuant to 42 U.S.C. § 2000e-16(b), it may apply the collateral source rule to decline to deduct insurance benefits that a claimant received through the Federal Employees Health Benefits program.

items.claim: The Equal Employment Opportunity Commission must apply the collateral source rule when awarding past pecuniary damages against a federal agency under 42 U.S.C. § 2000e-16(b), and is therefore required to decline to deduct insurance benefits received by a claimant through the Federal Employees Health Benefits program.

items.claim: Temporal proximity alone does not establish a causal connection between protected activity and termination when evidence of intervening performance concerns exists, and under a cat's paw theory of liability, a plaintiff must show that a lower-level supervisor's retaliatory animus was a but-for cause of, rather than merely a motivating factor in, the unbiased decision-maker's adverse employment decision.
items.case_holding_text:
we conclude that the trial court did not err when it found that there is

no genuine issue of material fact whether there was a causal connection between Ms. Whitney’s

protected activity and her termination. Although Ms. Whitney told the CEO about her concerns

with the compliance department only a couple of months before her termination, the CEO

concluded in his initial report that she should not be terminated. Only after he received additional

information, which did not include any additional allegations from Ms. Whitney, did he decide to
                                                   13


terminate her. As this Court noted in Lindsay, temporal proximity does not establish a causal

connection if there is evidence of intervening performance concerns. Lindsay, 2009-Ohio-1216,

at ¶ 13 (9th Dist.). Ms. Whitney’s second assignment of error is overruled.

                                 ASSIGNMENT OF ERROR III

       THE TRIAL COURT ERRED BY OVERLOOKING, WEIGHING AND OR
       FAILING TO CREDIT EVIDENCE IN REJECTING WHITNEY’S CAT’S PAW
       THEORY OF LIABILITY.

       {¶28} In her third assignment of error, Ms. Whitney argues that the trial court incorrectly

rejected her cat’s paw theory of liability. “A ‘cat’s paw’ is a person used by another to accomplish

the other’s purposes.” Smith v. Ohio Dept. of Pub. Safety, 2013-Ohio-4210, ¶ 55 (10th Dist.),

citing EEOC v. BCI Coca–Cola Bottling Co., 450 F.3d 476, 484 (10th Cir. 2006). Under this

theory, even if the person who made an adverse employment decision was unbiased, if a lower-

level supervisor had a retaliatory animus, the employer may be held liable. “The plaintiff must

show[,]” however, “that the lower-level supervisor’s discriminatory animus was a ‘but-for’ cause

of, or a determinative influence on, the unbiased superior’s adverse employment decision.” Id. at

¶ 62. Influence by a lower-level supervisor that was merely a motivating factor to the adverse

employment action is insufficient. Id. at ¶ 61.

       {¶29} Ms. Whitney argues that the trial court failed to recognize evidence in her favor.

She argues that the chief legal officer significantly altered the scope of the investigation being

carried out by outside counsel, including having it focus on the employee relations department’s

handling of IS complaints. She argues that the chief legal officer also requested that outside

counsel prepare a summary of its findings regarding the employee relations department, that she

items.claim: The existence of an employment relationship between a plaintiff and the business where she was assigned to work is a required element in an employment discrimination claim, and failure to establish such a relationship warrants summary judgment against the plaintiff.
items.case_holding_text: Grant of summary judgment was proper in employment discrimination case where plaintiff failed to show existence of employment relationship between herself and business where she was assigned to work by contractor.

items.claim: An employer's reliance on subjective supervisor evaluations as the sole basis for promotion decisions can constitute evidence of pretext in a Title VII disparate treatment claim, particularly where minority employees are disproportionately rated lower without documented performance criteria. The Fifth Circuit held that such practices, absent objective standards, are sufficient to survive summary judgment.
items.citation: Delacroix v. Harmon Freight Systems, Inc., 738 F.2d 614 (5th Cir. 1984)
items.case_name: Delacroix v. Harmon Freight Systems, Inc.

items.claim: An employer's reliance on facially neutral shift-scheduling criteria was found to constitute disparate impact discrimination where the practical effect fell overwhelmingly on employees of a protected religious minority. The Ninth Circuit held that operational convenience alone cannot justify a scheduling policy that foreseeably burdens Sabbath observers without meaningful accommodation alternatives.
items.citation: Wulfsberg v. Cascade Regional Transit Authority, 839 F.2d 412 (9th Cir. 1988)
items.case_name: Wulfsberg v. Cascade Regional Transit Authority

items.claim: An employer's reliance on subjective supervisor evaluations as the sole basis for promotion decisions may constitute evidence of discriminatory intent under Title VII when those evaluations disproportionately disadvantage employees of a protected racial class. The Seventh Circuit held that statistical disparity alone, when combined with documented supervisor bias, is sufficient to survive summary judgment.
items.citation: Okonkwo v. Pinnacle Aerospace Mfg. Corp., 78 F.3d 541 (7th Cir. 1996)
items.case_name: Okonkwo v. Pinnacle Aerospace Mfg. Corp.

items.claim: An employer's reliance on subjective criteria during promotion decisions, when applied inconsistently across racial groups, may constitute sufficient evidence of discriminatory intent to survive summary judgment. The Fifth Circuit held that statistical disparities combined with documented departures from stated hiring procedures can establish a prima facie case of race-based employment discrimination.
items.citation: Trevino v. Halcourt Medical Group, 739 F.3d 204 (5th Cir. 2014)

items.claim: An employer's reliance on subjective evaluation criteria, such as 'leadership presence' or 'cultural fit,' may constitute evidence of pretext for racial discrimination when those criteria are applied inconsistently across applicant pools. The Ninth Circuit held that statistical disparities in promotion rates, combined with vague evaluative language, were sufficient to survive summary judgment under Title VII.
items.citation: Pemberton v. Dillard Unified School District, 738 F.3d 214 (9th Cir. 2013)
items.case_name: Pemberton v. Dillard Unified School District
